headings.text: Using a variable before assignment; valid names
Constants — a special kind of variables

html:
The big picture

A Python variable is a name that refers to a value object; it gets created by the first assignment, and its type is simply the type of whatever it currently refers to (type annotations only document the intention). The memory model makes this concrete: every value is an object on the heap with metadata (reference count, type) plus the value, and the name lives in a dictionary (namespace) that points to it. So g = f copies a reference, and f = f * 2 creates a new object rather than changing the old one. The built-in scalar types (int, float, complex, bool, None, plus str for text) each come with literals and operators. Expressions combine them, and three rule sets decide what an expression means: precedence and associativity (how it is bracketed), type conversion (implicit promotion bool → int → float → complex, or explicit casting), and evaluation order (left to right, with lazy and/or).

Variables in Python

General aspects

In Python, a variable is created by assigning a first value to it (we invent its name). Its data type becomes the data type of the assigned value – the type can change at a subsequent assignment. (The address is managed automatically and is, in practice, irrelevant for programmers.)

x = 7          # Creates a variable named x that can
               # store whole numbers ➝ data type int
print(x)       # Prints 7 on the console
print(type(x)) # type() returns a character string holding
               # the variable's current type: <class 'int'>
x = "ISOP"     # Assigns a character string to the variable
               # ➝ thus changing its data type to str
print(x)       # Prints ISOP on the console
print(type(x)) # Prints <class 'str'>

In other languages (Java, C, C++ …), we must specify the name and the (fixed!) data type for variables before they are used – variable declaration: int x = 7; // x is int once and forever

Data type annotations

In Python, it is possible to annotate the intended data type when a variable is created. This resembles the variable declarations in other languages. The annotated version of the previous example:

x: int = 7        # Creates a variable named x of data type int
print(x)          # Prints 7 on the console
print(type(x))    # Prints <class 'int'>
x: str = "ISOP"   # Assigns a character string to x,
                  # changing its data type to str
print(x)          # Prints ISOP on the console
print(type(x))    # Prints <class 'str'>

*Side note on the slide: mypy flags the redefinition of a variable as an error.*

Type annotations are primarily intended for the program's readers. They are ignored during normal program execution, but they can be checked by external tools such as mypy to detect possible errors (https://mypy.readthedocs.io — install and use!).

Use type annotations wherever they clarify matters!

Common mistake — "the annotation makes x an int"

Tempting: after x: int = 7, Python will refuse x = "ISOP". It won't: the program runs, and type(x) becomes str, exactly as in the unannotated version. The annotation is a comment that tools can read. Only a checker such as mypy (run separately, before the program) complains: for the slide's second annotation x: str = … it reports Name "x" already defined (the redefinition the slide mentions), and for a plain x = "ISOP" after x: int = 7 it reports Incompatible types in assignment. The right model: the value has a type, the name doesn't.

Using a variable before assignment; valid names

Using a variable before the first value assignment results in an error:

print(number)  # NameError: name 'number' is not defined

Rules for a valid identifier (name) of a variable (these apply to all names in Python):

  • Combination of letters, digits and underscores (without spaces etc. and operators like +, -, *, etc.)
  • Must start with a letter or underscore
  • Identifiers are case-sensitive
  • Python keywords are not allowed (e.g., for, return)

  • We try to follow this naming convention (PEP 8, https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#prescriptive-naming-conventions):

    • variable names consist of lower case letters (and digits)
    • with words separated by underscores as necessary to improve readability: take, max_take, comp_turn …
Worked example — valid or not?

Apply the rules in order (allowed characters → first character → keyword → convention):

  • max_take — letters and _, starts with a letter, not a keyword → valid, PEP 8 style ✓
  • 2nd_try — starts with a digit → SyntaxError
  • comp-turn — - is an operator, so Python reads it as comp - turn → not a name (and a NameError if comp doesn't exist)
  • return — keyword → SyntaxError
  • MaxTake — valid, but breaks the convention (that style is for class names, later)
  • Take and take — two different variables (case-sensitive)

Assignment — shortcut assignment operators

Parallel assignment (actually sequence unpacking – see later):

x, y, z = 0, 0, 0  # x = 0; y = 0; z = 0

Compound assignment operators following the pattern •= (for any binary operator •):

a += b   # a = a + b
a -= b   # a = a - b
a *= b   # a = a * b
a /= b   # a = a / b
...

Advantages: simplification of writing; improved readability.

Why does a, b = b, a swap two variables without a helper variable?

Parallel assignment evaluates the whole right-hand side first (here: the pair of the current values of b and a) and only then assigns to the names on the left. So both old values are safe before anything is overwritten. The swap in 2 A First Contact with Python needed h because three separate assignments run one after another.

Constants — a special kind of variables

A constant is a variable the value of which cannot be changed. It should receive its value by a one-time assignment.

In Python, the property »being constant« (i.e., »being not re-assignable«) cannot be enforced; instead, we resort to a naming convention: constants should be named with uppercase characters only, with underscores separating words:

PI = 3.141592653589793
E = 2.718281828459045
ABSOLUTE_ZERO = -273.15

By using capital letters only, we communicate that the name is intended to be treated as a constant (as a variable that never changes). (https://realpython.com/python-constants/#what-constants-are)

In Java, constants are declared as »final« variables: final double PI = 3.1415926535; C++: const double PI = 3.1415926535; Changing them is inhibited by the compiler.

Built-in data types

Part I: scalars

Pre-defined data types (as opposed to user-defined objects) with scalar content (1 value per variable):

CategoryTypeValue rangeBytes
Whole numbersintunlimited (!)28; \ge 2^{30}: 32+
Floating point numbersfloat[-1.7 \times 10^{308} \,..\, +1.7 \times 10^{308}] ≙ float('-inf')..float('inf')24
Complex numberscomplex[same] + [same] j (2 float values, not quite scalar)32
Logical valuesbool{ False, True }28
Null valueNone{ None } – used to explicitly code »nothing«16

Variables typically contain addresses of value objects with metadata (see the memory model below).

In other languages (Java, C, C++ …), these types need no metadata. Thus, memory consumption is significantly less. E.g., int typically uses 4 bytes (!), with a value range of -2^{31} to -2^{31}-1 (long taking 8 bytes ranges from -2^{63} to 2^{63}-1) etc.

Unclear (slide 53)

The 4-byte int range is printed as "-2^{31} to -2^{31}-1"; the upper end should be +2^{31}-1 (= 2,147,483,647), matching the long range in the same sentence.

Memory model (64-bit architecture)

Memory layout for a float variable. Example: f = 3.14

  1. Python creates an object in memory to represent the value 3.14. This object has three parts:

    • the value: 3.14
    • the data type: float (a reference to type information)
    • the reference count: 1 – the number of variables or objects referring to this float
  2. Python creates a name ("f") in a dictionary and associates it with the object's reference.
  3. When we use (reference) a variable as in print(f), its name is looked up in the dictionary, and its value is used.

The name "f" lives in the Python interpreter's dictionary (namespace, e.g. globals()) and holds the address 5221000 of the float object. The object: refcnt 1 and type (a reference to the information on the data type float) are metadata, fval 3.14 is the value; 24 bytes in total. The objects a variable »points to« are allocated in a memory area called heap.

In future memory diagrams, memory addresses will be omitted, and references will be shown by arrows only. The linear table can also be split if this makes the diagram easier to understand.

In other languages, metadata can be omitted because data types are fixed, and therefore all type-related business is done by the compiler when it compiles the program and not at runtime! E.g., float (called double) in Java, C, or C++ typically uses 8 bytes (!), with the same value range as in Python (which uses 24 bytes). The variable f holds 3.14 directly — no indirection! The part of the main memory used for such variables is called stack.

Assignment to another variable. Example: g = f

Python: "g" gets the same reference as "f"; the reference count of the single 3.14 object is incremented to 2. C, C++, Java …: the content 3.14 is copied into g.

In Python, the reference is copied, not the value.

The value of these references can be inspected with id():

>>> f = 3.14
>>> id(f)
4310607088
>>> g = f
>>> g
3.14
>>> id(g)
4310607088
Intuition — id() is the arrow made visible

id(x) returns a number that identifies the object x refers to (in CPython, its memory address). Equal ids mean one object with two names, the arrows in the diagram above. The number itself changes from run to run, so only compare ids within one run. After f = f * 2 below, id(f) changes while id(g) stays the same.

Re-assignment of a variable. Example: f = f * 2

  1. Python computes the value and creates a new object in memory to represent the result 6.28.
  2. The name "f" is updated in the dictionary to reference the new object.
  3. The reference count for 3.14 is decremented. If it reaches 0, the object becomes eligible for garbage collection (re-insertion in the free memory heap for later re-use).

After f = f * 2: "g" still refers to 3.14 (refcount now 1), "f" refers to the new object 6.28. Inset top right: the state before (both names on 3.14, refcount 2). In other languages, the value of f is simply changed in place: f 6.28, g 3.14.

Intuition — name tags, not boxes

The prep course pictured variables as drawers that hold a value (3 Variables). For Python, a better picture is name tags on objects: f = 3.14 hangs the tag f on a 3.14 object; g = f hangs a second tag on the same object; f = f * 2 makes a new object and moves the tag f over to it. The old object keeps the tag g. An object with no tags left (refcount 0) can be thrown away.

Common mistake — "after g = f, changing f changes g"

Tempting conclusion from "they share one object": f = f * 2 must also double g. It doesn't: g is still 3.14, because re-assignment never modifies the object, it re-points the name (step 2 above). For numbers (and strings) the shared object can't be changed at all, so sharing is harmless. The situation where sharing really matters comes later, with types whose objects can be changed in place (lists).

Worked example — tracking reference counts

a = 1.5 → object 1.5, refcount 1 (tag a). b = a → same object, refcount 2 (tags a, b). a = a + 1 → new object 2.5 with refcount 1 (tag a); 1.5 drops to refcount 1 (tag b). b = 0.0 → new object 0.0 (tag b); 1.5 drops to refcount 0 → eligible for garbage collection. Result: a is 2.5, b is 0.0, and the 1.5 object is gone.

Why does Python need 24 bytes for a float that C stores in 8?

The value itself is the same 8-byte IEEE double. The other 16 bytes are the metadata: 8 for the reference count and 8 for the reference to the type information (both 64-bit numbers on a 64-bit machine). C doesn't need them because the compiler already knows each variable's type and checks it before the program runs; Python looks up types while the program runs, so every object must carry its type with it.

Whole numbers — int

Subset of \mathbb{W} (limited only by the memory available).

Literals:

  • decimal: -17, 4711, 1_000_000 (underscore for grouping instead of comma)
  • octal: 0o37 (31_{10}), 0o07
  • hexadecimal: 0xA39F (41887_{10})
  • binary: 0b1101 (13_{10})

Operations:

  • additive: +, - (binary and unary – sign!)
  • multiplicative: *, // (integral [floor] division), % (modulus, remainder)
  • exponentiation: **
  • comparisons: == (=), != (≠), >, <, >= (≥), <= (≤)
  • bit operations: | (disjunction, OR), & (conjunction, AND), ^ (antivalence, XOR), ~ (complement, NOT), <<, >> (shift)
Unclear (slide 58)

"Subset of \mathbb{W}": \mathbb{W} usually means the non-negative whole numbers \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}, but int includes negative numbers (the literal -17 on the same slide). The intended set is \mathbb{Z}, the integers.

Why do // and % belong together?

For whole numbers a and b \neq 0, Python guarantees a == (a // b) * b + a % b: // gives how many whole times b fits, % gives what is left over. E.g. 17 // 5 is 3 and 17 % 5 is 2, and 3 \cdot 5 + 2 = 17. Because // rounds down (towards -\infty), the remainder takes the sign of b: -7 // 2 is −4 and -7 % 2 is 1, since -4 \cdot 2 + 1 = -7.

Semantics of bit operations (excluding <<, >>)

The bits of the operands are combined individually. Example: a = 17 (00010001), b = 7 (00000111).

A one in the result will be exactly there, where…

  • disjunction: …either of the operands has a one — or = a | b # 23 (00010111)
  • conjunction: …both operands have a one — and = a & b # 1 (00000001)
  • antivalence: …the operands are different — xor = a ^ b # 22 (00010110)

  • complement: …the operand has a zero — notB = ~b # -8 (11111000 = −00001000)

    • Not well defined, since there are »infinite« leading zeroes. In fact, ~x := -x - 1.

Two's complement representation of negative numbers is used for bitwise operations – normally, negative numbers are represented as positive numbers with an explicit sign.

Unclear (slide 59)

The slide names its result variables or and and, but both are Python keywords, so or = a | b is a SyntaxError if you type it in. Use names like bit_or and bit_and.

Intuition — why ~7 is −8

Think of the bits of 7 as ...0000111 with infinitely many zeros in front. Flipping every bit gives ...1111000, infinitely many ones in front. In two's complement, "all ones" means −1, and ...1111000 is −1 minus the flipped-off 111 (= 7), i.e. -1 - 7 = -8. That is the rule ~x = -x - 1.

Semantics of shift operations (<<, >>)

The bits of the left operand are shifted by the number of digits specified by the right operand. Example: a = 17 (00010001), b = -8 (−00001000). You may think of the number »being shortened«.

  • Right shift: the rightmost bits are lost, zeroes are generated on the left side, the sign of the operand stays the same:

    • rSa1 = a >> 1 # 8 (00001000)
    • rSb2 = b >> 2 # -2 (−00000010)
    • Corresponds to an integral division // 2**(right operand)

  • Left shift: the leftmost bits are lost, zeroes are generated on the right side:

    • lSa2 = a << 2 # 68 (01000100)
    • lSb3 = b << 3 # -64 (−01000000)
    • Corresponds to a multiplication * 2**(right operand)
Worked example — reading off shifts as arithmetic

13 >> 2: write in binary 1101 → drop the 2 rightmost bits 11 → read back 3. Check with the rule: 13 // 2**2 = 13 // 4 = 3 ✓. 5 << 3: 101 → append 3 zeros 101000 → 40. Check: 5 * 2**3 = 40 ✓. Since Python's int is unlimited, no bits are really "lost" on the left in Python: 1 << 100 is simply 2^{100}.

Floating point numbers — float

Subset of \mathbb{R} in floating point representation (mantissa, exponent), IEEE 754 (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754):

\text{value} = \text{mantissa} \times \text{base}^{\text{exponent}}
Symbols
  • \text{mantissa} — the significant digits of the number, scaled to a fixed range (dimensionless)
  • \text{base} — the number system's base: 10 in the slide's example, but 2 in the actual computer representation
  • \text{exponent} — whole number saying how far the point is shifted (dimensionless); positive = larger, negative = smaller values

E.g., 179{,}23 = 0{,}17923 \times 10^3 (base in fact 2 instead of 10!).

Precision is limited: ~17 digits; smallest positive float number: 4{,}9 \times 10^{-324}.

Operations may yield inf (for »infinity«) or nan (for »not a number«). Riddle: give an example of an expression that yields inf or nan as its result.

Literals:

  • 0.23, -47.11, 3., .125 (decimal point needed to distinguish from int; _ allowed)
  • Scientific notation: -1.23e-45 (= -1.23 \times 10^{-45}) (infix e or E; decimal point optional)

Operations:

  • additive: +, - (binary and unary)
  • multiplicative: *, /, // (floor division), % (modulus, remainder) — e.g. 1.5 % 0.5 ➝ 0.0
  • comparison: == (attention – often imprecise!), !=, >, <, >=, <=
  • exponentiation: **

float corresponds to double in Java, C, C++ ➝ 64 bit.

Riddle: an expression that yields inf or nan?

1e308 * 10 overflows the largest float (about 1.8 \times 10^{308}) and gives inf. Then inf - inf (e.g. float('inf') - float('inf')) has no meaningful value and gives nan. Note what does not work: 1 / 0 and 1.0 / 0.0 raise ZeroDivisionError in Python instead of returning inf (unlike C or Java).

Common mistake — comparing floats with ==

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False, because neither 0.1 nor 0.2 has an exact binary form (see the Why on 452.37600000000003 in 2 A First Contact with Python). The fix is to compare with a tolerance: abs(x - y) < 1e-9, or math.isclose(x, y).

Complex numbers — complex

Subset of \mathbb{C} in floating point representation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number):

\text{real} + \text{im}\, j \quad \text{where } j^2 = -1
Symbols
  • \text{real} — real part (a float)
  • \text{im} — imaginary part (a float)
  • j — the imaginary unit, j^2 = -1 (Python and engineering write j; maths usually writes i)

Literals: -0.23 + 1.2j, 2j, 1j + 1 (all components of type float); imaginary part marked with j or J.

Operations:

  • additive: +, - (binary and unary)
  • multiplicative: *, /
  • comparison: == (attention – often imprecise!), != (no <, > etc.)
  • exponentiation: **
  • access to components: .real, .imag — (1j).real ➝ 0.0, (1j).imag ➝ 1.0
  • conjugate: .conjugate() — (1 - 2j).conjugate() ➝ (1 + 2j)

Many data types offer methods in addition to operators. Methods are functions operating on the value (instance) of the data type to the left of the dot.

Common mistake — j on its own

j alone is just a variable name (NameError if undefined). The imaginary unit must be written with a number in front: 1j. So 1 + j is 1 + 1j, not 1 + j.

Logical values — bool

Set {False, True} – boolean values often result from comparisons: a < b (true or false).

Literals: False, True

Operations (boolean algebra):

  • Negation: not (unary)
  • Conjunction (∧): and
  • Disjunction (∨): or
  • Comparison: ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= (False < True)
aba and ba or ba == ba != bnot a
FalseFalseFalse*False*TrueFalseTrue
FalseTrueFalse*True*FalseTrueTrue
TrueFalseFalse*True*FalseTrueFalse
TrueTrueTrue*True*TrueFalseFalse

* This is the »logical effect« of the operators and and or. Their real result, however, is one of their operands. E.g., or returns

  • a, if a is »truthy« (can be converted to True)
  • b, if a is »falsy«.

De Morgan rules:

  • not (a and b) ≡ not a or not b
  • not (a or b) ≡ not a and not b
Intuition — and mirrors or

Both operators return the operand that decided the result. or stops at the first truthy operand; and stops at the first falsy one. So a and b returns a if a is falsy, otherwise b. Examples: 0 or 5 → 5, 3 and 4 → 4, "" and "x" → "", None or 0 → 0. With real bool operands the result is always True/False, which is why the table above looks like plain logic.

Common mistake — x == 1 or 2

Tempting reading: "x is 1 or 2". Python reads (x == 1) or 2: for x = 3 the left side is False (falsy), so or returns its second operand 2, which is truthy. An if x == 1 or 2: therefore always runs. Write x == 1 or x == 2.

Connection

and/or/not and De Morgan are the propositional logic of 1 Elements of Logic (∧, ∨, ¬). Note a != b is exactly XOR on truth values, and a == b is the biconditional ↔.

Character strings — str

str is not a scalar data type and is therefore discussed in detail later. It is dealt with here because it is so useful for storing text.

Sequences of characters.

Literals: between " " or ' ' or """ """ or ''' '''

  • "Martin Hitz", "" (empty string), '\n' (string of length 1 with new line)

Operations:

  • + (concatenation): "Martin" + " Hitz" ≡ "Martin Hitz". To concatenate two literals, + may be omitted: "Martin" " Hitz" ≡ "Martin Hitz"
  • Comparison: ==, != as well as >, <, >=, <= (based on lexicographic ordering)

Stand-alone strings in a Python source code are ignored by the compiler ➝ strings are also used for multiline comments.

Common mistake — lexicographic is not alphabetical

Strings are compared character by character by their code numbers. All uppercase letters come before all lowercase ones, so "Zebra" < "apple" is True. Digits in strings are compared as characters too: "10" < "9" is True, because "1" comes before "9". Convert to numbers first if you mean numbers.

Expressions

Combining data

Expressions are used to calculate values.

  • Expressions are combinations of operands and corresponding operators.
  • Their evaluation yields a (typed) value.
  • Operands are subexpressions (possibly in parentheses), literals, variables or constants, and function or method calls (see later).

Example (arithmetic expression): a = 7; b = 3; c = a + 2 * b - 1

The slide shows the evaluation tree: (int) 2 * (int) 3 → (int) 6; (int) 7 + (int) 6 → (int) 13; (int) 13 - (int) 1 → (int) 12.

Resolution

The resolution of unbracketed expressions into subexpressions is determined by precedence and left/right associativity of the operators.

  • The precedence (priority) of the operators governs the implicit bracketing of subexpressions (e.g., »dot before dash«) – higher precedence binds stronger:

    • 3 + 4 * 2 ≡ 3 + (4 * 2)
    • x * y + 5 * z ≡ (x * y) + (5 * z)

  • Left/right associativity governs the implicit bracketing of subexpressions for operators at the same precedence level.

    • Right(-to-left) associativity: a • b • c ≡ a • (b • c)
    • Left(-to-right) associativity: a • b • c ≡ (a • b) • c
    • In Python, left associativity is the normal case: 7 - 3 - 2 ➝ 2 (not 6)

Precedence and associativity of operators

PrecedenceOperatorsAssociativity
1 (highest)(), [], .N/A / left
2awaitN/A
3**right
4+, -, ~ (unary)right
5*, @, /, //, %left
6+, - (binary)left
7<<, >>left
8&left
9^left
10|left
11==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, is, is not, in, not inchaining
12notright
13andleft
14orleft
15if – else (conditional expression)right
16lambdaN/A
17 (lowest):=N/A

Python interprets chained comparisons differently! a < b < c is not parsed as (a < b) < c, but as its mathematical interpretation (a < b) and (b < c), where b is evaluated only once! (That is the »chaining« in the associativity column of level 11.)

Intuition — the rows you'll actually meet

Level 1 is everything that "attaches" to an operand: brackets (), indexing [] and the dot . of a method call such as (1j).real. await (level 2, asynchronous code) and @ (matrix multiplication, level 5) belong to advanced topics this chapter doesn't use, and lambda comes later. For everyday expressions, remember the chain `> unary sign >* / // %> binary+ -> comparisons >not>and>or`**.

Why is ** right-associative and placed above unary minus?

Both follow mathematical notation. 2^{3^2} means 2^{(3^2)} = 2^9 = 512, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, not (2^3)^2 = 64. And -2^2 means -(2^2) = -4, so -2 ** 2 is −4 (the slide's last example below): ** (level 3) binds tighter than the sign (level 4). Write (-2) ** 2 if you mean 4.

Examples (precedence levels in brackets):

  • a + b < c + d ≡ (a + b) < (c + d) — [4] [11] [4]
  • a < b or c > d and a > d ≡ (a < b) or ((c > d) and (a > d)) — [11] [14] [11] [13] [11]
  • ab or not bb and cb ≡ ab or ((not bb) and cb) — [14] [12] [13]
  • -2 ** 2 ≡ -(2 ** 2) ≡ -4 — [4] [3]

When in doubt: use complete brackets (this also increases readability)!

Unclear (slide 68)

In the first example the binary + is labelled [4], but in the table on slide 67 level 4 is the unary +/-; binary +/- is level 6. The bracketing on the slide is right either way, because + (6) still binds stronger than < (11).

Worked example — bracketing step by step

x = 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2 // 5 - 1

  1. Highest level first (3): 4 ** 2 → 16. Now 2 + 3 * 16 // 5 - 1.
  2. Level 5, left to right: 3 * 16 → 48, then 48 // 5 → 9. Now 2 + 9 - 1.
  3. Level 6, left to right: 2 + 9 → 11, then 11 - 1 → 10. Fully bracketed: x = (2 + ((3 * (4 ** 2)) // 5)) - 1, so x is 10. Compare 3 * 16 / 5, which gives 9.6: the kind of division matters as much as the order.
Common mistake — not binds weaker than ==

not a == b means not (a == b) (level 11 before level 12), which is what you want. But a == not b is a SyntaxError; you must write a == (not b). And a < b < c is a chain: 1 < 3 > 2 is True (both comparisons hold), although it looks like nonsense.

Type compatibility and type conversions

Operands of an expression must be (data) type compatible to each other – each operation (+, *, …) ultimately requires operands of the same data type. Two types are compatible if they are

  • equal, or
  • one can be converted to the other by implicit type conversion (performed autonomously by the compiler).

Implicit (automatic) data type conversion (type promotion):

  • bool → int → float → complex (e.g., 3 + True ➝ 4)
  • All types used as arguments in the print() function → str

These conversions typically cause no data loss!

If no implicit type conversion is possible, an explicit conversion must take place. Since data loss is possible in this case, programmers must make it clear to the compiler that they know what they are doing…

Explicit data type conversions (type casting): Python offers the conversion functions such as int(), float(), str(), and bool() to explicitly convert a value to the respective type (where possible). Examples:

x = "123"       # String
y = int(x) * 2  # ➝ 246
print(bool(x))  # Any string except "" ➝ True

Loss of information — riddle: explain what is happening and why!

z = -7
print(int(z / 2), z // 2)  # -3 -4

A tricky way to implement a »default value«:

inp = int(input("Value: ") or "42")
Riddle: why does int(z / 2) give −3 but z // 2 give −4?

z / 2 is the float −3.5. int() cuts off the fractional part, i.e. rounds towards zero → −3. // floors, i.e. rounds towards -\infty → −4. For positive numbers both give the same result (int(7 / 2) and 7 // 2 are both 3), which is why the difference is easy to miss. The information lost is the .5, and the two operations lose it in different directions.

Why does input("Value: ") or "42" act as a default value?

or doesn't return True/False here; as slide 63 says, it returns the first operand if that is truthy, otherwise the second. An empty string "" is falsy (see bool("") above). So if the user just presses Enter, input() returns "", the expression becomes "42", and int("42") is 42. Any other input is passed on unchanged.

Common mistake — bool("False") is True

bool() on a string only asks "is it empty?". bool("False"), bool("0") and bool(" ") are all True; only bool("") is False. To turn user input like "yes"/"no" into a truth value, compare it: answer == "yes".

Evaluation order

Subexpressions are evaluated (with respect to time) strictly from left to right. (The order is especially important if side effects occur in the expression – see later.)

Logical expressions are »lazily« evaluated (conditional evaluation, lazy evaluation) – only as long as the final result is not yet determined:

  • x and y yields always False, if x == False
  • x or y yields always True, if x == True

Therefore, y is not evaluated in these cases. Riddle: which algebraic law for the operators and and or is violated because of this?

Improves robustness: y may contain illegal code (in case 1 when x == False and in case 2 when x == True, respectively). Example:

(x != 0 and y / x > 2)  # never leads to division by 0
Riddle: which algebraic law is violated?

Commutativity. In logic, x \land y \equiv y \land x. In Python, x != 0 and y / x > 2 is safe for x = 0 (result False), but the swapped y / x > 2 and x != 0 evaluates the division first and raises ZeroDivisionError. The truth value is commutative whenever both sides can be evaluated; the behaviour is not.

The evaluation order is especially important if side effects occur in the expression!

Example 1:

two_inputs = input("#1") + input("#2")
print(two_inputs)

Here, the second keyboard input is concatenated to the first (and not vice versa):

#1Martin
#2 Hitz
Martin Hitz

Assignment expressions

Inside an expression, one can save the value of a subexpression to a variable using the so-called walrus operator :=.

The value of the expression var := subexpression is just the value of the subexpression. However, as a side effect, this value is also assigned to the variable var.

In languages of the C family (Java, C, C++ …), assignment expressions can be formulated using the standard assignment operator =.

Example: given a cylinder with radius r and height h, let us calculate the volume:

cyl_vol = r ** 2 * 3.14159 * h

If we are also interested in the area of the basis, we can save this value in base_area:

cyl_vol = (base_area := r ** 2 * 3.14159) * h
Common mistake — forgetting the brackets around :=

:= has the lowest precedence of all (level 17). Without brackets, cyl_vol = base_area := r ** 2 * 3.14159 * h is a SyntaxError, and inside a bigger expression n := a * h would capture the whole product, not just a. Always bracket the part you want to save, as the slide does. For r = 2, h = 5 the bracketed version gives base_area ≈ 12.566 and cyl_vol ≈ 62.83.

Example 2 (evaluation order):

i = 2
j = (i := 3) * i  # j = 9

If evaluation from right to left were possible, j could also receive the value 6 (= old value of i multiplied by the result of the assignment).

Avoid expressions where the evaluation order is crucial!
